Ask for the Gap, Not the Summary

Playbooklowob research

By Chris WellsFrom lowob RESEARCH · 25 August 2026 · 6-minute read · Strategy

A good judgment system does not ask people to tell it everything. It knows what the next decision will need, notices what it is missing, and asks for exactly that, of the person most likely to know. The method is simple: write a needs template for each decision class, compare the live record against it, rank the gaps, and ask only the top one. One sharp question is answered in seconds. Five are an interrogation, and the research on alert fatigue shows what people do with too many prompts.

The default capture prompt is "summarise the meeting". It produces long, generic text in which the one thing that mattered is buried or absent. People learn quickly that nobody reads the summary, and they stop writing good ones.

The better pattern is gap-seeking, and it is more tractable to build than it sounds.

Why the summary fails

Summaries fail for two reasons, one about machines and one about people.

For the machine, more text is not more context. Anthropic's engineering guidance treats context as "a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns", cites research showing recall falls as context grows, and advises finding "the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of your desired outcome." A long meeting summary is the opposite: many tokens, little signal, and the critical fact somewhere in the middle. Our explainer on context engineering covers the mechanics.

For people, a summary records what was discussed, and what was discussed is mostly what everyone already knew. Stasser and Titus's 1985 experiments found group discussion centres on shared information, while facts held by only one member are rarely raised. A summary of that discussion inherits the bias. The item that would change the next decision is often the one nobody said aloud. Conversation intelligence tools can transcribe everything; they cannot record what was never said.

How to compute a gap

Every decision class has an implicit list of what a good decision needs. Make that list explicit as a template for each class, in the same spirit as the structured fields of a decision record: Martin Fowler's architecture decision record and the UK government's 2025 framework both specify the fields up front so that nothing important depends on someone remembering to include it.

Decision classWhat a good decision needs
RenewalBudget holder, usage trend, competitive threat, relationship temperature, open support issues, contract terms
Credit reviewRecent financials, loan-condition status, ownership changes, sector view, covenant headroom
Discount exceptionDeal size, standard terms, precedent for similar exceptions, approver, competitive pressure
PartnershipPartner's incentive, exclusivity terms, owner on each side, exit terms, first milestone

Then, after any interaction touching a live decision, compare the record's current state with the template. The difference is the gap list. The ten decision types in The ten commercial decisions worth recording are a reasonable place to start writing templates.

Rank, then ask one

Rank gaps by three things: how much the next decision depends on the item, how stale the current information is, and how cheap it is to answer. Ask only the top one.

Gap in a renewal recordDecision depends on itStalenessCost to answerAsk now
Budget holder after the reorganisationHighSix months oldOne sentenceYes
Competitor in the accountHighThree months oldOne sentence, may be unknownNext time
Usage trendMediumAvailable from product dataZero, fetch itFetch, do not ask
Relationship temperatureMediumTwo weeks oldOne wordNo

The discipline of one question is not politeness. It is what keeps the questions answered. In a review of 17 studies, Heleen van der Sijs and colleagues found clinicians overrode drug safety alerts in roughly 49% to 96% of cases. Among the system flaws they identified were low specificity, unclear information and unnecessary disruption to work. A capture system that sends five questions after every call is building the same habit. Gartner's 2023 survey of 501 sellers found 77% struggled to complete their assigned tasks efficiently; a question queue adds to that load unless every question earns its place.

A single, sharp question is answered in seconds. Five questions feel like an interrogation and get skipped.

Good gap questions are specific and answerable

"Did the budget holder change after the reorganisation?" "Was the objection about price, or about timing?" "Is the March waiver of the loan condition still in force?"

Each can be answered in a few words. "I don't know" is a valid answer and itself useful: it marks an item the next person should verify, not assume.

Route the question to whoever knows. Gap-seeking does not have to ask the person who just finished the interaction. The system often knows who touched the account last, who owns the relationship, or who analysed the sector. Route the question to the person most likely to answer it well. Given what the group research shows about knowledge held by one person, this is often the only way that knowledge reaches the record. It turns the system from a form into something closer to a well-informed colleague who knows who to ask.

Gaps that recur are schema problems

Track which gaps appear most often across records. A gap that recurs across many decisions is usually a field the schema lacks, or a source the system is not connected to. In the ranking table above, usage trend should never be a question: it is a data connection waiting to be made. Recurring gaps are the cheapest product research you will ever get, because the system is telling you, in aggregate, what it does not know.

Mind the tone. A system that only ever asks what is missing can feel like an auditor. Pair every gap question with a give: the precedent, the warning, the drafted brief. And never ask the same person more than one gap question per interaction. Our review of AI notetakers for decision capture covers which tools can be configured to work this way.

What would prove this wrong

Records built from free-form summaries proving as complete and as useful for later decisions as records built from targeted gap questions, at similar cost in time. Then the summary is good enough. This is testable: run both on one decision class for a quarter and compare how often each record answered the questions asked of it later.

lowob takeaways

  • Template first. Write the six to ten things a good decision in each class needs.
  • Compare, rank, ask one. Dependence, staleness and cost to answer decide which gap comes first.
  • Route to whoever knows. The person who just left the meeting is not always the right one.
  • Fix recurring gaps in the schema. A question asked every week is a missing field or connection.

Common questions

What is gap-seeking in a knowledge or decision system?

Instead of asking for a summary, the system compares a decision record with a template of what that decision class needs and asks for the single most important missing item.

How many follow-up questions should a system ask after a meeting?

One. A single sharp question is answered in seconds, while several feel like an interrogation and get skipped. Never ask the same person more than one gap question per interaction.

Who should a gap question go to?

The person most likely to answer it well, such as whoever last touched the account, owns the relationship or analysed the sector, not necessarily the person who just finished the interaction.

Why are AI meeting summaries often useless?

They record what was discussed, which is mostly what everyone already knew, and they bury the one item that matters in long text. A targeted question about the missing item is shorter and more useful.

Sources and notes

  • Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents, 29 September 2025. Vendor engineering guidance.
  • Stasser and Titus, Pooling of unshared information in group decision making, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 48(6), 1985. Laboratory experiment with student groups.
  • van der Sijs, Aarts, Vulto and Berg, Overriding of drug safety alerts in computerized physician order entry, JAMIA 13(2), 2006. Peer-reviewed review of 17 clinical studies; an analogue, not a study of business capture tools.
  • Gartner, Survey finds 77% of sellers struggle to complete their assigned tasks efficiently, 2 November 2023. Analyst survey of 501 sellers; self-reported.
  • Martin Fowler, Architecture Decision Record, 24 March 2026. Practitioner reference.
  • GOV.UK, Architectural Decision Record framework, 4 November 2025. Public-sector standard.
